headline: The two datasets give opposite answers to *does search help?*. On **airports**, a B variant has the highest F1 for four of five models (B + memory 0.21–0.32, B search up to 0.29, against 0.16–0.24 for A best); deepseek ties (B + memory 0.24 vs A best 0.23). On **football**, A best has the highest F1 for four of five models (0.19–0.43 against 0.12–0.23 for B + memory), and only gpt-oss:120b ties. The same agent, models and prompts were used on both, so the difference comes from the data: airport facts (codes, cities, runways) are published in a few standard sources, while player statistics depend on season and competition.
delta: Going from airports to football, Strategy B loses F1 for every model (search −0.02 to −0.16, memory −0.01 to −0.12), while Strategy A gains for the two models that answer most (mistral and deepseek: A best +0.19/+0.20). F1 ign of A rises on football for most models (+0.05 to +0.35), because football has many properties with typical values that pass the numeric tolerance. Abstention rises on football for B (+0.04 to +0.28) and for A zero-shot of the three cautious models (+0.27 to +0.43).
pr: Plotting every configuration shows the shift. On airports the B points (diamonds and triangles) sit above and to the right of their model's A prompts for the gpt-oss models and mistral. On football they sit below and to the left of the A cloud for every model. Strategy A's points move to higher precision and, for mistral and deepseek, to much higher recall on football.
variance: For F1, the choice of model matters more than the choice of prompt on both datasets. The span over models is 0.07 (airports) and 0.28 (football) with context on, against 0.01 and 0.09 over prompts. With abstentions ignored, the picture flips on football: prompts span 0.22, more than models (0.10). Prompts mostly change *how accurate the answers given are*, while models mostly change *how many tasks are answered*.
prompt_consistency: The ranking of model × prompt configurations transfers only partly between datasets (Spearman ρ = 0.47 for F1) and not at all for F1 ign (ρ = 0.01). On airports the mean rank of the 9 prompts is flat (4.4–6.2); on football the few-shot prompts are clearly best (5-shot mean rank 2.8, 3-shot 3.2) and zero-shot clearly worst (7.8). A prompt chosen on one graph should not be assumed best on another.
context: Context behaves differently on the two datasets. On airports, the 85 task pairs where context-on tasks replace some of the airport's own properties with properties of neighbouring nodes lose F1 for every model (−0.05 to −0.16, all significant). For F1 ign the loss is significant for mistral (−0.06) and deepseek (−0.12). On football's 33 pairs no model shows a significant change. Context properties are a weaker clue than the node's own properties, especially on airports, where an own property like the city or the ICAO prefix nearly identifies the airport.
ab_forest: Task by task, B − A is mostly positive on airports and mostly negative on football. On airports, B search beats A zero-shot significantly for gpt-oss:20b, gpt-oss:120b and mistral (+0.11 to +0.14 F1), and B + memory beats A best for gpt-oss:20b (+0.10) and gpt-oss:120b (+0.09). On football, B is significantly worse than A best for gemma4, mistral and deepseek (−0.10 to −0.36), and the only significant gains of B are over the zero-shot prompt of the cautious models.
memory: Allowing memory on the same evidence is a safer gain on football than on airports. On football, F1 rises for every model (+0.04 to +0.07) with modest drops in abstention. On airports, F1 rises for gemma4 (+0.05) and deepseek (+0.08), is unchanged for the gpt-oss models and falls for mistral (−0.03), even though abstention falls by 9–17 points. With abstentions ignored, memory lowers precision for three models on airports and raises it for all five on football: on airports the evidence is usually better than the model's memory, on football it is not.
retrieval: The agent identifies the entity much more often on airports. Its plan names an entity in 31–59% of airport runs (8–20% the right airport), against 11–17% of football runs (10–12% the right player, almost only when the name is given). Airports give the agent usable search keys (codes, cities, coordinates) where football's given properties are season statistics. Answer rates follow: 27–52% of airport runs answer, against 8–30% on football.
domains: Both datasets draw evidence from a long tail (1,955 domains for airports, 1,174 for football; the top 5 hold 26% and 30% of the evidence slots). The cited sources differ in quality: on airports, en.wikipedia.org and ourairports.com account for most citations and are reference sources for exactly the stored facts. On football, the citations spread over statistics aggregators (fbref, footystats, transfermarkt, footymetrics) that disagree by season and competition.
strata: The popularity of the hidden property orders difficulty on airports but not on football. On airports, F1 rises from the low to the high H stratum for both A best (0.05 → 0.31) and B + memory (0.10 → 0.43), and the gain from search is largest for popular properties. On football the H strata are flat or inverted (A best 0.25–0.36, B + memory 0.17–0.22). G and node-centrality strata give no consistent pattern on either dataset.
difficulty: The difficulty score works as intended on airports, where the easiest tertile scores highest for every approach (A best 0.28, B + memory 0.34). On football it does not: the hardest tertile scores highest for every approach (A best 0.40, B + memory 0.24). The difficulty measure, built from popularity and centrality, captures how rare the information is in the graph, not how hard it is to guess or retrieve. On football these two diverge.
popularity: Per property, popularity explains much of the airports scores: the one low-popularity property (commercial_flights, pop = 0.10) is the hardest. Football's properties cluster at pop ≈ 0.06 (goalkeeper statistics) and ≈ 0.79 (outfield statistics) with scores from 0 to above 0.9 inside each cluster.
energy: The cost structure is the same on both datasets. A run of B takes 0.36–1.75 Wh, most of it in web searches, against 0.001–0.13 Wh for the model's best A prompt (roughly 10–400×). Token amplification is 5.6–7.2× for B and 1.1–3.9× for A. On airports this extra energy buys a higher F1 for four models; on football it buys a lower F1 for four.
stability: Run-to-run stability is similar on both datasets: on average over the models, the 3 runs agree on the outcome for 67–71% of the tasks with B, 60–69% with the A best prompt and 79–83% with A zero-shot. The lower stability of A best comes from the compact prompt, which several models prefer and which is the least stable.
takeaways:
1. **Whether search helps depends on the dataset.** B + memory beats the best A prompt on airports for 4 of 5 models (F1 0.21–0.32 vs 0.16–0.24) and loses to it on football for 4 of 5 (0.12–0.23 vs 0.19–0.43).
2. **Entity identification decides B's success.** The agent names the right node in 8–20% of airport runs but 10–12% of football runs, and on football almost only when the name is given.
3. **The model matters more than the prompt for F1 on both datasets** (span 0.07–0.28 vs 0.01–0.09), but prompt rankings transfer poorly between datasets (ρ = 0.47 for F1, 0.01 for F1 ign).
4. **Context hurts on airports and is neutral on football** when it replaces the node's own properties (airports ΔF1 −0.05 to −0.16 for all models).
5. **The difficulty measure transfers poorly.** Popularity orders airport tasks but not football tasks, where guessable typical values dominate.
6. **Memory is a consistent, cheap improvement for B on football** (+0.04 to +0.07 F1 for all models) and a mixed one on airports.
7. **B costs roughly 10–400× the energy of A** and amplifies the user's input 6–7×, on both datasets.
